pos: v.i. (to cease to live; rendering Hebrew muth, Greek apothnesko)
etymology: From the Norse deyja, to die. Hebrew muth is the plain verb, and the first threat in Scripture doubles it — moth tamuth, dying thou shalt die — an intensive the Authorized Version renders thou shalt surely die.
biblical_def: Die in Scripture is never merely biological. The first sentence pronounced on man makes death the wages of a specific act, and the Hebrew doubles the verb for emphasis: in the day thou eatest thereof, dying thou shalt die. Ezekiel states the principle of personal guilt in its plainest form: “Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4). Paul gives the doctrine its final shape — the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life. The word also governs the fences round the holy: the Kohathites “shall not go in to see when the holy things are covered, lest they die” (Numbers 4:20). David refuses to hasten Saul's end and leaves the manner of it to God: “the LORD shall smite him; or his day shall come to die; or he shall descend into battle” (1 Samuel 26:10). And Proverbs uses the word to steady an anxious parent: “Withhold not correction from the child: for if thou beatest him with the rod, he shall not die” (Proverbs 23:13).
webster_summary: To cease to live. In Scripture death is the wages of sin rather than a natural necessity — the soul that sinneth, it shall die — and the first threat in the Bible doubles the Hebrew verb: dying thou shalt die.
webster_full: DIE, v.i. [Norse deyja.] To cease to live; to expire; to decease.
2. To be punished with death; as, the soul that sinneth, it shall die.
3. To perish; to come to an end; as, the memory of the wicked shall die.
4. To languish; to sink; as, his heart died within him.
5. In Scripture, thou shalt surely die, Gen. 2; the soul that sinneth, it shall die, Ezek. 18.
corruption_summary: Death is presented in modern speech as a natural part of life, a stage in a journey, or a merciful release. Scripture calls it an enemy and traces it to a cause — sin — and only that diagnosis makes room for a remedy.
corruption_paragraphs: The naturalising of death is comforting and false. Paul calls death the last enemy that shall be destroyed, and Christ at the grave of Lazarus groaned in the spirit and wept, which is not how anyone responds to a natural process. Genesis presents death as an intrusion into a creation pronounced very good, entering by one man's transgression and passing upon all men. A culture that cannot say why men die is left either denying death or aestheticising it, and both leave the dying with nothing to hold.

Ezekiel 18:4 also forecloses the opposite comfort, which is inherited righteousness. The chapter is answering a proverb the exiles were using — the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge — and God refuses it: the soul that sinneth, it shall die. Original sin makes every man guilty in Adam and corrupt by nature; it does not permit any man to blame his parents for his own transgressions. The Christian answer to death is neither denial nor fatalism but substitution: Christ tasted death for every one of His people, and the sting was drawn at the cross.
roots_summary: Hebrew muth is to die, and its infinitive absolute construction gives the emphatic surely die; maveth is death itself. Greek apothnesko is to die off, and thanatos is death, the last enemy.
roots_lines: Hebrew muth (H4191) — to die, to be put to death; the plain verb of mortality and of judicial execution.
Hebrew moth tamuth — dying thou shalt die; the doubled infinitive of Genesis 2:17, rendered thou shalt surely die.
Hebrew maveth (H4194) — death; personified in Hosea 13:14, O death, I will be thy plagues.
Greek apothnesko (G599) — to die off, to expire; the ordinary New Testament verb.
Greek thanatos (G2288) — death; called by Paul the last enemy to be destroyed.
usage: Of personal guilt admitting no inheritance of innocence: the soul that sinneth, it shall die (Ezekiel 18:4).
Of a fence set about holy things: they shall not go in to see when the holy things are covered, lest they die (Numbers 4:20).
Of correction that a parent need not fear: if thou beatest him with the rod, he shall not die (Proverbs 23:13).
scriptures: Ezekiel 18:4
Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.
Romans 6:23
For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
Numbers 4:20
But they shall not go in to see when the holy things are covered, lest they die.
Proverbs 23:13
Withhold not correction from the child: for if thou beatest him with the rod, he shall not die.

pos: v.i. (to have life, to be restored; rendering Hebrew chayah, Greek zao)
etymology: From Saxon libban, to live. Hebrew chayah means both to live and to be made alive — to revive — and the second sense governs the most important occurrences, where dead things are commanded to live.
biblical_def: Live in Scripture is very often not the continuation of life but its restoration. The most striking instance is in the valley of dry bones, where the verb is put into a command addressed to the dead: “Thus saith the Lord GOD unto these bones; Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live” (Ezekiel 37:5). Bones cannot cooperate, and the prophet is told to preach to them anyway — which is the whole doctrine of regeneration in a picture. Wisdom issues the same kind of summons: “Forsake the foolish, and live; and go in the way of understanding” (Proverbs 9:6). Elisha's word to the widow whose oil has been multiplied is entirely practical: “Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy children of the rest” (2 Kings 4:7) — debt paid first, then living. Paul ties the believer's life to Christ's: “Now if we be dead with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him” (Romans 6:8). And Abram's use of the word in Egypt is a low one — his soul shall live because of a half-truth about his wife.
webster_summary: To have life; and in Scripture very often to be made alive again. The verb is addressed to dry bones, to the foolish, and to those dead with Christ — in each case life comes as a gift commanded from outside.
webster_full: LIVE, v.i. [Sax. libban.] To exist; to have life; to be capable of the functions of life.
2. To be restored to life; to revive; as, these bones shall live.
3. To subsist; to be supported; as, live thou and thy children of the rest.
4. To pass life in a particular manner; as, to live in the fear of God.
5. In Scripture, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live, Ezek. 37; Forsake the foolish, and live, Prov. 9.
corruption_summary: The command live is addressed in Scripture to the dead, which is why regeneration cannot be a human decision. The modern gospel appeal frequently assumes the opposite: a living man choosing among options.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 37 is the decisive picture. The prophet is set down in a valley full of very dry bones and asked whether they can live; he answers, wisely, O Lord GOD, thou knowest. He is then commanded to prophesy to them, and the life comes as the word is preached. Nothing in the bones contributes. The New Testament says the same without the figure: you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins. A dead man is not weakened, or undecided, or in need of encouragement; he is dead, and only a creative word will do.

This does not make preaching pointless; it makes preaching the instrument. God commands the prophet to speak to bones, and He commands the church to preach to sinners, and the Spirit gives life through the word preached. So the free offer stands, and men are genuinely summoned — Forsake the foolish, and live. What changes is where the credit lies and how the preacher works: not by contriving a decision, but by declaring the word and asking God to do what only He can do. And the pastoral comfort is considerable, since no case is too far gone for a God who speaks to bones.
roots_summary: Hebrew chayah is to live or to revive, whence chay, living, and chayyim, life; Greek zao is to live and zoopoieo to make alive, the verb of quickening.
roots_lines: Hebrew chayah (H2421) — to live, to revive, to be made alive; the verb commanded over the dry bones.
Hebrew chayyim (H2416) — life; a plural noun, as though life were too full a thing for the singular.
Greek zao (G2198) — to live; used of natural life and of the life given in Christ.
Greek zoopoieo (G2227) — to make alive, to quicken; the Spirit's work in regeneration.
Greek zoe (G2222) — life; the word in eternal life, distinguished from bios, the course of living.
usage: Of life commanded over the dead: I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live (Ezekiel 37:5).
Of wisdom's summons to the simple: Forsake the foolish, and live (Proverbs 9:6).
Of union with Christ in His death and life: if we be dead with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him (Romans 6:8).
scriptures: Ezekiel 37:5
Thus saith the Lord GOD unto these bones; Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live:
Proverbs 9:6
Forsake the foolish, and live; and go in the way of understanding.
Romans 6:8
Now if we be dead with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him:
2 Kings 4:7
Then she came and told the man of God. And he said, Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy children of the rest.

pos: n. and v. (aid, succour; rendering Hebrew 'ezer and 'azar, Greek boetheia)
etymology: From Saxon helpan, to aid. Hebrew 'ezer is a strong word, used far more often of God than of men — the God who helps Israel in battle — which is why its use in Genesis 2:18 of the woman carries no suggestion of inferiority.
biblical_def: Help in Scripture is chiefly something God gives and men cannot manufacture. The pilgrim psalm asks and answers the question in two lines: “I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help” — and then, refusing the hills themselves — “My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth” (Psalm 121:1-2). The negative is put as sharply: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psalm 146:3). A prophet tells Amaziah that hired troops will not decide the matter, “for God hath power to help, and to cast down” (2 Chronicles 25:8). And the psalmist reports a divine appointment in language the New Testament takes up of Christ: “I have laid help upon one that is mighty; I have exalted one chosen out of the people” (Psalm 89:19) — help not merely given but laid upon a person, a Champion appointed for a people who could not save themselves.
webster_summary: Aid or succour; and in Scripture chiefly the aid of God, who alone finally helps. The Hebrew word is used far more often of God than of men, and the psalms set it directly against trust in princes and in armies.
webster_full: HELP, v.t. [Sax. helpan.] To aid; to assist; to lend strength or means towards effecting a purpose.
2. To relieve; to succour; to save from difficulty or distress.
3. HELP, n. Aid; assistance; that which gives strength or relief.
4. One who aids or assists; a helper; as, an help meet for him.
5. In Scripture, My help cometh from the LORD, Psa. 121; in whom there is no help, Psa. 146.
corruption_summary: Self-sufficiency is the culture's cardinal virtue, and asking for help is treated as a defect. Scripture assumes creaturely dependence as the normal condition and treats the refusal to look outside oneself as the actual defect.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is dependence. Psalm 121 begins with a man looking to the hills — possibly to the high places where the nations sought their gods — and correcting himself in the next breath: his help comes from the Maker of heaven and earth, not from the hills or from what is on them. The correction is the psalm. It is the same instinct Isaiah rebukes in those who went down to Egypt for horses, and the same one Psalm 146 names in the trust reposed in princes.

The doctrine has a horizontal side that the same texts require. God's help ordinarily arrives through means and through people: the Levite who assists, the brother who bears a burden, the church that supplies a want. Paul, who wrote that God comforts the cast down, adds that He did so by the coming of Titus. So dependence on God is not a reason to refuse human help but the ground for receiving it without shame, since the giver is an instrument and not the source. What Scripture forbids is not accepting help but resting in it — making the prince, the army, or the friend the thing trusted.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'azar is to help or succour, whence 'ezer, a help, and the names Ebenezer and Azariah; Greek boetheo is to run to a cry, and boetheia is the help so rendered.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'azar (H5826) — to help, succour, support; used overwhelmingly of God helping His people.
Hebrew 'ezer (H5828) — a help or helper; the noun in an help meet for him and in Ebenezer, the stone of help.
Hebrew teshu'ah (H8668) — deliverance, salvation; what a horse is a vain thing for, in Psalm 33:17.
Greek boetheo (G997) — to run to a cry for aid; the verb of the centurion and of the Syrophenician woman.
Greek boetheia (G996) — help, succour; let us come boldly unto the throne of grace... to help in time of need.
usage: Of the source of help identified and corrected: My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth (Psalm 121:2).
Of trust withheld from human power: Put not your trust in princes... in whom there is no help (Psalm 146:3).
Of help laid upon an appointed champion: I have laid help upon one that is mighty (Psalm 89:19).

A Song of degrees. I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help.
Psalm 121:2

Psalm 146:3

Psalm 89:19

pos: v.t. (to present, to sacrifice; rendering Hebrew qarab in the causative, Greek prosphero)
etymology: From Latin offerre, to bring before — ob, before, and ferre, to bear. Hebrew qarab means to draw near, and its causative means to cause to draw near; the offering is what a man brings when he approaches, and its noun qorban is simply that which is brought near.
biblical_def: Offer is to bring near, and the Hebrew makes plain what the English hides: an offering is the means by which a man approaches. The great day of the year begins with the high priest offering for himself before he can act for anyone else: “Aaron shall offer his bullock of the sin offering, which is for himself, and make an atonement for himself, and for his house” (Leviticus 16:6) — a mediator who must first be covered. The princes bring the dedication gifts of the altar in turn, each on his day (Numbers 7:11). The feast offerings are specified to the animal and the blemish: “ye shall offer a burnt offering for a sweet savour unto the LORD; one young bullock, one ram, and seven lambs of the first year without blemish” (Numbers 29:2). And promptness is commanded with the firstfruits, since a delayed offering says something about the giver. Isaiah 57:7 shows the word turned to idolatry: Judah went up a high mountain to offer sacrifice, the same verb serving a false altar.
webster_summary: To present or bring near, especially in sacrifice. The Hebrew root means to draw near, so that an offering is what a man brings in order to approach — and the high priest had to offer for himself before he could offer for the people.
webster_full: OFFER, v.t. [L. offero; ob and fero, to bear.] To present for acceptance or rejection; to bring before.
2. To present in worship; to sacrifice; as, to offer a burnt offering.
3. To present verbally; to propose; as, to offer terms of peace.
4. OFFERING, n. That which is presented in divine service; an oblation.
5. In Scripture, Aaron shall offer his bullock of the sin offering, Lev. 16; ye shall offer a burnt offering for a sweet savour, Num. 29.
corruption_summary: The mass, offered as a propitiatory sacrifice, contradicts the finality Hebrews insists on; and at the other extreme, a worship that offers nothing at all forgets that approaching God has always cost the worshipper something.
corruption_paragraphs: The Roman doctrine that the mass is a true and proper sacrifice offered for the living and the dead is answered directly by the argument of Hebrews. The Levitical priests standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins; but this man, after He had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down. The sitting is the proof. A sacrifice that must be re-presented is a sacrifice that did not finish, and the Reformation identified this as one of the central corruptions to be renounced. Christ is not offered again; He is remembered, and He is fed upon by faith.

The opposite failure is real too. Where the finished work is rightly held, congregations sometimes conclude that nothing is now brought at all. Scripture says otherwise: we are to offer the sacrifice of praise continually, to present our bodies a living sacrifice, and to do good and communicate, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased. What is abolished is the propitiatory offering, not the grateful one. And Psalm 51 names the offering God will not despise, which no ritual can substitute for: a broken spirit, a broken and a contrite heart.
roots_summary: Hebrew qarab is to draw near; in the causative it means to bring near or offer, and its noun qorban is an offering. Greek prosphero is to bear toward, and prosphora is the oblation.
roots_lines: Hebrew qarab (H7126) — to draw near; in the causative, to bring near, to offer.
Hebrew qorban (H7133) — an offering; literally that which is brought near, the word Christ cites in Mark 7:11.
Hebrew 'olah (H5930) — a burnt offering; literally that which ascends, wholly consumed on the altar.
Greek prosphero (G4374) — to bear toward, to offer; the verb of Christ's one offering in Hebrews 10:12.
Greek hapax (G530) — once, once for all; the adverb that settles the finality of that offering.
usage: Of a mediator who must first be covered himself: Aaron shall offer his bullock of the sin offering, which is for himself (Leviticus 16:6).
Of offerings specified without blemish: ye shall offer a burnt offering for a sweet savour unto the LORD (Numbers 29:2).
Of the same verb turned to idolatry: even thither wentest thou up to offer sacrifice (Isaiah 57:7).
scriptures: Leviticus 16:6
And Aaron shall offer his bullock of the sin offering, which is for himself, and make an atonement for himself, and for his house.
Numbers 29:2
And ye shall offer a burnt offering for a sweet savour unto the LORD; one young bullock, one ram, and seven lambs of the first year without blemish:
Isaiah 57:7
Upon a lofty and high mountain hast thou set thy bed: even thither wentest thou up to offer sacrifice.
Psalm 51:17
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.

pos: v.t. and n. (to order with authority; rendering Hebrew tsavah, Greek entellomai)
etymology: From Latin com, with, and mandare, to commit or enjoin. Hebrew tsavah is to lay a charge upon someone, and its noun mitzvah is a commandment — the standing word for what God has enjoined and for what a father enjoins his household.
biblical_def: Command is to lay a charge with authority, and Scripture uses the word of God, of Moses, and of parents, in that descending order of derivation. God's commanding is not arbitrary and, Moses insists, not obscure: “For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off” (Deuteronomy 30:11). Nor may it be adjusted: “What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deuteronomy 12:32). Human commands derive from and are limited by it. Rebekah's charge to Jacob — “obey my voice according to that which I command thee” (Genesis 27:8) — is a mother using rightful authority to procure a deception, and the family never recovers. The Pharisees press Christ on the divorce certificate: “Why did Moses then command to give a writing of divorcement?” (Matthew 19:7), and His answer distinguishes what Moses suffered for hardness of heart from what was commanded from the beginning. And Christ leaves His own commandment, which is love (John 15:12).
webster_summary: To order or enjoin with authority; and the charge so given. In Scripture God's commandment is neither hidden nor far off, and may be neither added to nor diminished; human authority to command is derived from His and bounded by it.
webster_full: COMMAND, v.t. [L. com and mando, to commit, to enjoin.] To bid; to order; to direct with authority.
2. To govern; to lead; to have under direction or control.
3. COMMAND, n. The right or power of governing with chief authority; an order given.
4. COMMANDMENT, n. A command; a mandate; a precept of the divine law.
5. In Scripture, this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, Deut. 30; This is my commandment, John 15.
corruption_summary: Two errors attend the word: the claim that God's commands are too obscure to be obeyed, and the treatment of derived human authority — parental, ecclesiastical, civil — as though it were absolute rather than answerable.
corruption_paragraphs: Moses forecloses the first in advance. The commandment is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off; it is not in heaven, nor beyond the sea, but very nigh, in the mouth and in the heart. Where Scripture is genuinely difficult the difficulty is real, and the Confession acknowledges that not all things are alike plain; but it insists that those things necessary to be known, believed, and observed for salvation are so clearly propounded that the unlearned may attain a sufficient understanding of them. An appeal to obscurity is very often an evasion, and the words a man understands are usually the ones he most wishes he did not.

The second error is the more dangerous because it wears the language of obedience. Rebekah commanded Jacob, and had a mother's right to command, and used it to procure a lie; Jacob obeyed and spent twenty years in exile for it. All human authority is derived, and therefore bounded: the apostles answered the council that we ought to obey God rather than men, and Scripture nowhere requires submission to a command that God forbids. Parents, elders, and magistrates all rule under a Lawgiver, and the man who commands must answer for the command as surely as the man who obeys must answer for the obedience.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsavah is to lay a charge upon, and its noun mitzvah is a commandment; Greek entellomai is to enjoin, and entole is the commandment, the word in this is my commandment.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsavah (H6680) — to lay a charge upon, to command, to appoint; used of God, of Moses, and of parents.
Hebrew mitzvah (H4687) — a commandment; the standing noun for a precept of the divine law.
Greek entellomai (G1781) — to enjoin, to give charge; the verb behind the Great Commission's all things whatsoever I have commanded you.
Greek entole (G1785) — a commandment; the noun in This is my commandment, That ye love one another.
Latin mandare — to commit, to enjoin; the root of command and of mandate.
usage: Of a commandment neither hidden nor distant: it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off (Deuteronomy 30:11).
Of a law that may be neither supplemented nor reduced: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it (Deuteronomy 12:32).
Of Christ's own commandment to His disciples: This is my commandment, That ye love one another (John 15:12).
scriptures: Deuteronomy 30:11
For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off.
Deuteronomy 12:32
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
Genesis 27:8
Now therefore, my son, obey my voice according to that which I command thee.
John 15:12
This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you.

pos: adj. and v.t. (laid waste, forsaken; rendering Hebrew shamem, Greek eremos)
etymology: From Latin desolare, to leave alone — de, entirely, and solus, alone. Hebrew shamem carries both the ruin of a place and the horror of those who look at it; the same root gives the word rendered astonished.
biblical_def: Desolate means laid waste and left alone, and Hebrew joins the two ideas that English separates: shamem describes both the wasted land and the appalled onlooker. God warns Israel that even conquest must be gradual, lest the country empty out faster than it can be settled: “I will not drive them out from before thee in one year; lest the land become desolate, and the beast of the field multiply against thee” (Exodus 23:29) — a mercy in the form of a delay. Jeremiah pronounces the sentence on Judah with a limit attached: “The whole land shall be desolate; yet will I not make a full end” (Jeremiah 4:27), the clause on which the whole doctrine of the remnant hangs. Ezekiel says the same to Edom without that clause: “I will lay thy cities waste, and thou shalt be desolate” (Ezekiel 35:4). And the word describes a man as well as a country. Lamentations 3:11 is one of the loneliest sentences in Scripture: “He hath turned aside my ways, and pulled me in pieces: he hath made me desolate” — written by a man who, twelve verses later, says the LORD's mercies are new every morning.
webster_summary: Laid waste; forsaken; left alone. The Hebrew word covers both the ruined place and the horror of those who behold it. Jeremiah's sentence on Judah carries the clause on which the remnant doctrine hangs: yet will I not make a full end.
webster_full: DESOLATE, a. [L. desolatus; de and solus, alone.] Destitute of inhabitants; laid waste; ruined.
2. Solitary; without a companion; afflicted; as, a desolate widow.
3. DESOLATE, v.t. To lay waste; to ruin; to deprive of inhabitants.
4. DESOLATION, n. Destruction; ruin; a place laid waste; also, gloominess of mind.
5. In Scripture, The whole land shall be desolate; yet will I not make a full end, Jer. 4; he hath made me desolate, Lam. 3.
corruption_summary: Judgment in Scripture is almost never total, and the qualifying clauses are regularly overlooked by readers on both sides — by those who find the prophets merely vindictive, and by those who preach ruin without the remnant.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the doctrine of the remnant. Jeremiah's sentence is severe and its qualification is deliberate: the whole land shall be desolate; yet will I not make a full end. Isaiah says that except the LORD of hosts had left a very small remnant, Israel would have been as Sodom; Paul takes up the same word to describe his own generation — even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace. God has never once left Himself without a witness, and He has usually left fewer than anyone expected and more than anyone could see.

Lamentations 3 shows what this means for a person rather than a nation, and it is worth reading in order. The man who writes he hath made me desolate has already said that God has broken his bones, walled him about, and filled him with bitterness; he is not managing his feelings. And then, without retracting a word of it, he says: This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. The hope is not a denial of the desolation. It is recalled deliberately, in the middle of it, which is the only place such hope is ever needed.
roots_summary: Hebrew shamem means both to be laid waste and to be appalled; shemamah is a wasteland. Greek eremos is desert or deserted, and eremosis gives the abomination of desolation.
roots_lines: Hebrew shamem (H8074) — to be desolate, to be appalled; one root for the ruin and for the horror at it.
Hebrew shemamah (H8077) — a wasteland or desolation; the state of a land emptied of inhabitants.
Hebrew she'ar (H7605) — a remnant, that which is left; the qualification on nearly every sentence of ruin.
Greek eremos (G2048) — desert, solitary, deserted; used of the wilderness and of a house left desolate.
Greek eremosis (G2050) — desolation; the noun in the abomination of desolation.
usage: Of a conquest slowed in mercy: lest the land become desolate, and the beast of the field multiply against thee (Exodus 23:29).
Of judgment with the remnant clause attached: The whole land shall be desolate; yet will I not make a full end (Jeremiah 4:27).
Of a man's own condition under affliction: he hath made me desolate (Lamentations 3:11).
scriptures: Exodus 23:29
I will not drive them out from before thee in one year; lest the land become desolate, and the beast of the field multiply against thee.
Jeremiah 4:27
For thus hath the LORD said, The whole land shall be desolate; yet will I not make a full end.
Lamentations 3:11
He hath turned aside my ways, and pulled me in pieces: he hath made me desolate.
Ezekiel 35:4
I will lay thy cities waste, and thou shalt be desolate, and thou shalt know that I am the LORD.

pos: adv. (widely, out of doors, in foreign parts; rendering Hebrew puts in the causative, Greek ekchuno and diaphemizo)
etymology: A compound of a (on) and broad — at large, over a wide space. In Scripture it attaches to three verbs above all: scattering, spreading, and making known, and the same idea of dispersion serves for judgment and for mission.
biblical_def: Abroad means at large or widely, and its biblical uses turn on dispersion. It records the spread of the nations from Babel onward: “afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad” (Genesis 10:18). It carries the covenant threat of exile: “If ye transgress, I will scatter you abroad among the nations” (Nehemiah 1:8) — which Nehemiah quotes back to God in prayer, along with the promise attached to repentance. Ezekiel uses it of shepherds who scatter the flock they were given to feed: “ye have thrust with side and with shoulder, and pushed all the diseased with your horns, till ye have scattered them abroad” (Ezekiel 34:21). But the word is also the vehicle of the gospel's spread: the shepherds at Bethlehem “made known abroad the saying which was told them concerning this child” (Luke 2:17), and Paul writes that “the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost” (Romans 5:5). What judgment scatters, grace also spreads.
webster_summary: At large; widely; out of doors or in foreign parts. In Scripture it attends the scattering of nations in judgment, the exile threatened for transgression, and equally the spreading abroad of the gospel and of the love of God in the heart.
webster_full: ABROAD, adv. [a and broad.] At large; widely; over a wide space.
2. Out of the house; as, he is gone abroad.
3. In foreign countries; beyond the borders of one's own land.
4. Extensively; before the public; as, the report is spread abroad.
5. In Scripture, I will scatter you abroad among the nations, Neh. 1; the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts, Rom. 5.
corruption_summary: Scattering appears in Scripture as a judgment, and yet God repeatedly turns it into the means of blessing — Babel into the nations, exile into the synagogues of the dispersion, and the persecution of Acts 8 into the first missionary expansion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is that God overrules judgment for mission. The scattering from Babel was a sentence on human pride, and it produced the nations to which the gospel was afterward sent. The exile was the covenant curse executed, and it planted Jewish communities across the empire, which became the first synagogues Paul preached in. Acts 8 states the pattern most compactly: a great persecution arose, and they were all scattered abroad — and the next clause is that they that were scattered went everywhere preaching the word.

Ezekiel 34 keeps the doctrine from becoming a comfortable fatalism. The shepherds who scattered the flock are not excused because God brought good out of it; they are indicted, and the chapter ends with God declaring that He will Himself seek out His sheep and set one shepherd over them. Providence overruling a sin never lessens the sin. Joseph put both truths in one sentence to his brothers — ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good — and both halves have to be said.
roots_summary: Hebrew puts in the causative is to scatter or disperse; pazar is to scatter as seed. Greek diaspeiro gives diaspora, the dispersion, and ekchuno is to pour out, the verb of Romans 5:5.
roots_lines: Hebrew puts (H6327) — to scatter, disperse, break up; the verb of Babel and of the exile.
Hebrew pazar (H6340) — to scatter, as seed is scattered; used both of dispersion and of liberality.
Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad; whence diaspora, the dispersion of Israel.
Greek ekchuno (G1632) — to pour out; the verb behind shed abroad in our hearts.
Greek diaphemizo (G1310) — to spread abroad a report; used of the news of Christ's miracles.
usage: Of the nations dispersed after Babel: afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad (Genesis 10:18).
Of the exile threatened in the covenant: If ye transgress, I will scatter you abroad among the nations (Nehemiah 1:8).
Of the gospel and the love of God spread widely: made known abroad the saying which was told them (Luke 2:17).
scriptures: Genesis 10:18
And the Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite: and afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad.
Nehemiah 1:8
Remember, I beseech thee, the word that thou commandedst thy servant Moses, saying, If ye transgress, I will scatter you abroad among the nations:
Ezekiel 34:21
Because ye have thrust with side and with shoulder, and pushed all the diseased with your horns, till ye have scattered them abroad;
Luke 2:17
And when they had seen it, they made known abroad the saying which was told them concerning this child.

pos: adv. (wholly, entirely; rendering the Hebrew infinitive absolute and charam, Greek holos)
etymology: From utter, outermost or complete, from Saxon utera, outer. In the Authorized Version it very often renders the Hebrew infinitive absolute — a verb doubled for emphasis — and elsewhere the verb charam, to devote a thing irrevocably to destruction.
biblical_def: Utterly means wholly, without remainder, and it is the translators' usual device for the Hebrew habit of doubling a verb for emphasis. It is used of a father's absolute refusal in the law of seduction: “If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins” (Exodus 22:17) — the daughter protected by a right of veto that money cannot override. It is used of God's promise to destroy idols without exception, in a sentence of four words: “And the idols he shall utterly abolish” (Isaiah 2:18). It is used of judgment on nations that will not serve (Isaiah 60:12). And in one of the great sentences of the Old Testament it is used in the negative, of what God refused to do to a people who had earned it: “Nevertheless for thy great mercies' sake thou didst not utterly consume them, nor forsake them; for thou art a gracious and merciful God” (Nehemiah 9:31).
webster_summary: Wholly; entirely; without remainder. In Scripture it commonly renders the Hebrew doubling of a verb for emphasis, and its most important use is a negative one: God did not utterly consume a people who deserved it.
webster_full: UTTERLY, adv. [from utter, Sax. utera, outer.] Fully; completely; entirely; wholly.
2. Without exception or remainder; as, utterly destroyed.
3. It renders the Hebrew infinitive absolute, in which a verb is doubled for emphasis.
4. UTTER, a. Complete; total; final; as, utter ruin.
5. In Scripture, the idols he shall utterly abolish, Isa. 2; thou didst not utterly consume them, Neh. 9.
corruption_summary: The absolute language of judgment is read as evidence of a cruel God, while the equally absolute language of mercy in the same books goes unread. Nehemiah 9 holds both, and holds them in the right order.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 9 is a national confession, and it is unsparing about the nation. It rehearses centuries of rebellion — they were disobedient, they cast the law behind their backs, they slew the prophets — and it does not soften a single item. Then comes the clause: Nevertheless for thy great mercies' sake thou didst not utterly consume them, nor forsake them; for thou art a gracious and merciful God. The mercy is not asserted instead of the guilt but on top of it, and it is grounded in God's character rather than in any extenuating circumstance. That is the shape of every honest confession.

The absolute language of destruction has its own context and it is judicial. Charam, the verb behind much of it, means to devote irrevocably — a thing placed beyond recovery or use, whether for destruction or for the sanctuary. The Canaanite cities were so devoted after four centuries of divine forbearance, for practices Leviticus 18 catalogues, and Israel was warned she would be treated the same and afterward was. What Scripture never does is present God as capricious. The forbearance is always longer than anyone would grant, and the judgment always later than anyone would defer it.
roots_summary: Hebrew emphasises by the infinitive absolute, doubling the verb (dying thou shalt die); charam means to devote irrevocably, giving the noun cherem, a devoted thing. Greek uses holos and pantelos for completeness.
roots_lines: Hebrew infinitive absolute — a verb repeated in the absolute form for emphasis, usually rendered by surely or utterly.
Hebrew charam (H2763) — to devote irrevocably, to ban; used of cities and spoil placed beyond recovery.
Hebrew cherem (H2764) — a devoted thing, a ban; the noun behind the Achan narrative in Joshua 7.
Hebrew kalah (H3615) — to complete, to consume entirely; the verb God did not carry out in Nehemiah 9:31.
Greek pantelos (G3838) — completely, to the uttermost; able also to save them to the uttermost.
usage: Of an absolute paternal refusal protecting a daughter: If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him (Exodus 22:17).
Of idols abolished without exception: And the idols he shall utterly abolish (Isaiah 2:18).
Of mercy withholding a deserved end: thou didst not utterly consume them, nor forsake them (Nehemiah 9:31).
scriptures: Exodus 22:17
If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins.
Isaiah 2:18
And the idols he shall utterly abolish.
Nehemiah 9:31
Nevertheless for thy great mercies' sake thou didst not utterly consume them, nor forsake them; for thou art a gracious and merciful God.
Isaiah 60:12
For the nation and kingdom that will not serve thee shall perish; yea, those nations shall be utterly wasted.

pos: adv. (in like manner, also; rendering Hebrew ken and gam, Greek homoios and hosautos)
etymology: A compound of like and wise (manner) — in like manner. It is the word by which a rule already stated is extended to a second case, and in the Gospels it repeatedly extends a warning or a judgment from one party to the hearer.
biblical_def: Likewise means in the same manner, and it is the hinge on which a stated principle is applied to a further case. The law uses it to extend a rule from one kind of firstling to another: “Likewise shalt thou do with thine oxen, and with thy sheep” (Exodus 22:30). Chronicles uses it of the Levites' duty morning and evening alike (1 Chronicles 23:30). But the Lord's uses are the arresting ones, because they turn a parable back on the hearer. He ends the parable of the unmerciful servant: “So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses” (Matthew 18:35) — the fictional king's severity applied without softening to the men listening. And twice in Luke 13, after news of Galileans killed by Pilate and of eighteen crushed by a tower, He refuses the question of comparative guilt and turns it on the crowd: “except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish” (Luke 13:5). The word denies every hearer the position of spectator.
webster_summary: In like manner; also. It extends a stated rule to a further case, and in the Gospels it repeatedly turns a parable or a piece of news back on the hearer — so likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you.
webster_full: LIKEWISE, adv. [like and wise, manner.] In like manner; also; moreover; too.
2. It extends to a second case what has been said of the first.
3. It answers to the Greek homoios and hosautos, in like manner.
4. It is used both to add a particular and to apply a principle.
5. In Scripture, So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, Matt. 18; except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish, Luke 13.
corruption_summary: Scripture is regularly read as though it were about other people. Likewise is the word that closes that escape: the parable's king, the tower at Siloam, the fate of the Galileans — each is turned on the man hearing.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 13 shows the mechanism plainly. The crowd brings Christ a news item with a theological question attached: were these Galileans, whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices, worse sinners than others? It is a comfortable question, because it invites a verdict on somebody else. He answers I tell you, Nay and adds the clause they did not ask for: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. Then, so that no one can attribute the first case to Roman politics, He supplies a second — the tower in Siloam, an accident with no villain — and repeats the sentence word for word.

The parable of the unmerciful servant closes the same way. A hearer may enjoy the story's justice from a distance, since the servant in it is plainly monstrous; then comes So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, with the qualification if ye from your hearts forgive not. James describes the alternative as a man beholding his natural face in a glass and going away and forgetting straightway what manner of man he was. The discipline the word enforces is simply to read every passage as addressed to oneself first, and to ask what must change here before asking who else needs to hear it.
roots_summary: Hebrew extends with ken (so, thus) and gam (also); Greek uses homoios and hosautos, both meaning in like manner. The English compound joins like to wise, an old noun meaning manner.
roots_lines: Hebrew ken (H3651) — so, thus, in like manner; the ordinary particle of comparison.
Hebrew gam (H1571) — also, moreover; adds a further case to one already stated.
Greek homoios (G3668) — likewise, in like manner; the word in Luke 13:3 and 13:5.
Greek hosautos (G5615) — in the same way; used in the household codes of the epistles.
Saxon wise — manner, way; the noun surviving in likewise, otherwise, and nowise.
usage: Of a rule extended from one firstling to another: Likewise shalt thou do with thine oxen, and with thy sheep (Exodus 22:30).
Of a parable turned on the hearer: So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you (Matthew 18:35).
Of news refused as a verdict on others: except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish (Luke 13:5).
scriptures: Exodus 22:30
Likewise shalt thou do with thine oxen, and with thy sheep: seven days it shall be with his dam; on the eighth day thou shalt give it me.
Matthew 18:35
So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.
Luke 13:5
I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.
1 Chronicles 23:30
And to stand every morning to thank and praise the LORD, and likewise at even;

pos: conj. (when in fact, considering that, in contrast to; rendering Hebrew 'asher and ya'an, Greek hoti and hos)
etymology: A compound of where and as. It sets two states of affairs side by side, either to mark a contrast (whereas I was blind, now I see) or to introduce a premise (whereas it was in thine heart) — the second sense surviving in the preambles of legal instruments.
biblical_def: Whereas sets two things side by side, and in Scripture it produces some of the sharpest contrasts in the canon. The healed blind man of John 9, badgered by the authorities to condemn the One who healed him, gives the answer that has served plain believers ever since: “Whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see” (John 9:25). He concedes the theology he does not know and holds the fact he does. The word also marks the gap between what was and what is under judgment: “ye shall be left few in number, whereas ye were as the stars of heaven for multitude” (Deuteronomy 28:62). It marks restoration in the same form reversed: “the desolate land shall be tilled, whereas it lay desolate in the sight of all that passed by” (Ezekiel 36:34). In its other sense it introduces a premise, as when the LORD commends David's intention though refusing his request: “Whereas it was in thine heart to build an house unto my name, thou didst well that it was in thine heart” (1 Kings 8:18).
webster_summary: A conjunction setting two states side by side, either in contrast (whereas I was blind, now I see) or as a premise (whereas it was in thine heart). It carries the healed man's testimony in John 9 and the LORD's commendation of David's intention.
webster_full: WHEREAS, conj. [where and as.] When in fact; the thing being so; considering that.
2. It introduces a premise or recital, as in the preamble of a law or a deed.
3. It marks a contrast or opposition between two states or facts.
4. It belongs to the class of compound relatives with whereof, whereby, wherein.
5. In Scripture, whereas I was blind, now I see, John 9; Whereas it was in thine heart to build an house, 1 Kings 8.
corruption_summary: The healed man's testimony is often used to make experience the final authority, as though what a person has felt settles what is true. He said the opposite: he distinguished carefully between what he knew and what he did not.
corruption_paragraphs: John 9:25 is a model of honest witness precisely because of what it refuses to claim. Pressed to pronounce Jesus a sinner, the man does not bluff: whether he be a sinner or no, I know not. He confines himself to what he can testify — he was blind, and now he sees — and that fact is enough to defeat every argument brought against him, because it will not go away. A Christian's testimony has the same shape and the same limits: it establishes what God has done in him, and it does not by itself establish doctrine.

The modern inversion makes experience the arbiter of truth, so that this is what I have lived ends a discussion rather than contributing to it. Scripture reverses the order: the Bereans searched the Scriptures daily to see whether the things preached were so, and Paul says that if an angel from heaven preach another gospel, let him be accursed. Experience is real evidence of God's work and is never the standard by which His word is judged. The blind man, notably, does not settle the christological question at all — Christ finds him later and reveals Himself, and only then does he worship.
roots_summary: Hebrew uses 'asher and ya'an (because, forasmuch as) for the premise sense, and simple juxtaposition for contrast; Greek uses hoti and hos. The English compound joins where to as.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'asher (H834) — who, which, that; the general relative, doing duty for several English conjunctions.
Hebrew ya'an (H3282) — because, forasmuch as; introduces the ground of a judgment or a promise.
Greek hoti (G3754) — that, because; introduces the fact asserted in John 9:25.
Greek tuphlos (G5185) — blind; the condition the man testifies to having left.
Greek blepo (G991) — to see, to look; now I see, the one thing he claimed to know.
usage: Of testimony confined to what the witness knows: whereas I was blind, now I see (John 9:25).
Of a multitude reduced under judgment: ye shall be left few in number, whereas ye were as the stars of heaven (Deuteronomy 28:62).
Of an intention commended though the request was refused: Whereas it was in thine heart to build an house unto my name (1 Kings 8:18).
scriptures: John 9:25
He answered and said, Whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see.
Deuteronomy 28:62
And ye shall be left few in number, whereas ye were as the stars of heaven for multitude; because thou wouldest not obey the voice of the LORD thy God.
Ezekiel 36:34
And the desolate land shall be tilled, whereas it lay desolate in the sight of all that passed by.
1 Kings 8:18
And the LORD said unto David my father, Whereas it was in thine heart to build an house unto my name, thou didst well that it was in thine heart.
